displayQuote: Success always obsoletes the very behavior that achieved it

meta.title: Who really said "Success always obsoletes the very behavior that achieved it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Drucker: the line appears in Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973), p. 88 — unusual, since his most-quoted lines are often fakes.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Success always obsoletes the very behavior that achieved it'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes — Peter Drucker really wrote it, in Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973), p. 88. Most famous 'Drucker' quotes aren't his. This one is.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The line is from Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (Harper & Row, 1973) — Wikiquote’s sourced list ↗ places it in Part 1, at p. 88 — and the Drucker Institute publishes the full surrounding paragraph under Drucker’s name. Unusually for a widely-shared Drucker line, this one is real.

source.heading: The book

docMeta.dd: Part 1, p. 88 — per Wikiquote’s sourced list

source.excerpt: Success always obsoletes the very behavior that achieved it. It always creates new realities.
trail: Wikiquote’s Drucker page ↗ carries this sentence in its sourced list — not the attributed or misattributed ones — under the heading for Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (New York: Harper & Row, 1973), in Part 1, at p. 88.

The Drucker Institute at Claremont Graduate University ↗ published the full paragraph under Drucker’s name on 7 September 2011, in a column by Joseph Maciariello that reads it alongside Schumpeter’s creative destruction.

The same institute keeps a public catalogue of Drucker’s most famous mis-quotations ↗ — and this line is not on it. Maciariello was the Institute’s founding academic and research director, so the same shop that debunks the fakes is the one that printed this passage as genuine.
Quote Investigator’s Drucker archive ↗ runs to eight investigations, several of them debunkings. This sentence is not among them; no fact-checker has needed to take it apart.
source.excerptNote: Drucker goes on to say that success also generates its own fresh problems, and that the hardest company in which to reopen the question ‘what is our business?’ is a successful one. The full paragraph is reproduced by the Drucker Institute ↗.
source.rightsHolder: The estate of Peter F. Drucker and Harper & Row, the original publisher
source.rightsNote: The sentence comes from Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices, first published by Harper & Row in 1973 — decades after the 1931 US public-domain cutoff — so the book and this line remain in copyright. Quoting a sentence for identification and comment is ordinary fair use; the Internet Archive scan ↗ is lending-restricted for the same reason.

author.name: Peter Drucker
author.heading: Peter F. Drucker
author.metaLine: 1909–2005 · Austrian-American management writer, consultant and educator
author.bio: Peter Ferdinand Drucker (1909–2005) was an Austrian-American writer, consultant and teacher who did more than anyone to make management a subject you could study rather than merely practise. From 1971 until his death he was Clarke Professor of Social Science and Management at Claremont Graduate University, which now houses the Drucker Institute and his personal archive. Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973) was his broadest single statement of the discipline, and the book this sentence comes from.

misattribution.heading: Drucker’s fake-quote problem
misattribution.intro: Peter Drucker is one of the most heavily counterfeited names in business writing — so heavily that the institute bearing his name keeps a running public list of lines he never wrote. This sentence is not on that list. But it travels in bad company, and it is worth knowing which of its neighbours are forgeries.

items.why: The Drucker Institute ↗ calls this his most enduring mis-quotation. What he actually argued, in a 1991 Wall Street Journal piece the Institute cites, was that culture is stubbornly persistent — not that it defeats every attempt to change it.

Also on the Institute’s list ↗, which points to a longer sentence in People and Performance about choosing what to measure — and notes that the snappy version strips out the role Drucker gave managers in making any tool work.

items.scope: “Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things.”
items.why: The Institute nicknames it “the Moby Dick of Drucker mis-quotations” and reports that Warren Bennis, once thought to be the co-source, could only say it sounded like something either of them might have said. See the entry ↗.

items.scope: “The best way to predict the future is to create it.”
items.why: Another entry on the same list ↗; the Institute says the phrasing is probably best credited to the computer scientist Alan Kay.

misattribution.truthLine: This line is the exception. Wikiquote files it among Drucker’s sourced quotations ↗, at p. 88 of Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices, and the Drucker Institute prints the full paragraph under his name. Credit it to Drucker — and cite the book, because almost nobody who reposts it does.

context.heading: Why the sentence bites
lead: Most warnings about complacency say some version of ‘don’t rest on your laurels.’ Drucker’s claim is sharper and less comfortable: the winning behaviour is precisely the thing the win destroys. Succeed, and the market, the workforce and the customer base you now face are not the ones your playbook was written for — so the playbook is already out of date on the day it pays off.

In the paragraph the line opens, Drucker goes straight from that observation to his signature question — what is our business? — and argues that the company least able to ask it honestly is the successful one, because nobody wants to argue with a win. The Drucker Institute’s 2011 column on the passage ↗ traces the thinking to Joseph Schumpeter, a friend of the Drucker family and one of the biggest influences on his work, and to Schumpeter’s idea of creative destruction.
context.detailsSummary: What the Institute draws out of the passage
detailsBody: Writing for the Institute, Joseph Maciariello reads the sentence through the S-curve: products and organisations pass through growth, stagnation and decline, and the moment to rethink the business is near the top of the curve, while there is still surplus to absorb the hit of investing in something new.
His practical conclusion is the uncomfortable one — be willing to cannibalise your own successful products and services, because if you do not, a competitor will. Read the column ↗.
context.pull: The winning behaviour is not merely superseded by success. It is obsoleted by it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section lists "Success always obsoletes the very behavior that achieved it." at p. 88, Part 1, under the heading 'MANAGEMENT: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (1973)', with the header note 'Peter F. Drucker, Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices, New York: Harper & Row, 1973.'

The Drucker Institute column 'Joe's Journal: On Success and Creative Destruction' (dated 09.07.2011, by Joe Maciariello) opens with the full paragraph beginning 'Success always obsoletes the very behavior that achieved it. It always creates new realities...' signed '-Peter F. Drucker', and frames it via Schumpeter's creative destruction and the S-curve.

The Drucker Institute's 'Did Peter Drucker Say That?' page catalogues his most famous mis-quotations - including 'Culture eats strategy for breakfast', 'The best way to predict the future is to create it' (credited instead to Alan Kay), 'What gets measured, gets managed' (real sentence traced to People and Performance), and 'Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things' (called 'the Moby Dick of Drucker mis-quotations', with the Warren Bennis remark) - and it does not contain the string 'obsoletes'. It also identifies Joseph Maciariello as the Institute's founding Academic and Research director.
Quote Investigator's Peter Drucker category lists eight investigations and none of them concerns 'Success always obsoletes the very behavior that achieved it'.

Peter Drucker was born 19 November 1909 and died 11 November 2005; he was an Austrian-American management consultant, educator and author; he was Clarke Professor of Social Science and Management at Claremont Graduate University from 1971 until his death; and 'Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices' was published in 1973 by Harper & Row.
The Internet Archive holds a lending-restricted scan of Peter F. Drucker's 'Management: tasks, responsibilities, practices' (New York, Harper & Row) under this identifier.
